edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Make every shape a different way.
edits.fix: The page has two different shapes (two small hexagons, 2 tilings; three long 2-1-1 hexagons, 3 tilings), so 'every shape a different way' is unclear. Say instead: 'Cover the two small hexagons in different ways, and the three long hexagons in different ways.'

k-1.summary: A concrete, non-watered-down K–1 set with every board at actual size. It includes impossible boards, among them an 8-triangle trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down triangles; fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4); all tilings of hexagons (2, 3 and 6 ways, with exactly that many boards); fewest blocks (3, 3, 4); and a blue-block game whose winners (1, 2, 1, 1, 2) all check out. Only the P3 wording and the footer need changing.

edits.quote: The gray triangles are holes, so they are not part of the board. Cover each board with blue rhombuses, or decide that it cannot be done. For each board that cannot be covered, explain why.
edits.fix: This repeats P1's task word for word. Merge E–G into Problem 1 as one shared question over two pages ('boards A–G on this page and the next'), and keep only the sentence 'Gray triangles are holes.'

grades-2-3.summary: A well-sequenced development of the up/down coloring argument, and every board checks. A, D and G can be tiled; B has an odd count; C has 7 up and 5 down; E has two up-triangle holes; F is balanced but its two halves meet only at a point. Then come fewest greens 2–5 with a proof prompt, the chevron comparison (4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5), a board-invention task, and a rule-finding problem whose rule (one up, one down) holds for all 144 such placements. The only edits are the P1/P2 repetition and the footer.

edits.quote: Give each of your coverings in Problem 1 a letter.
edits.fix: Children will naturally use A–F, which clash with the printed coverings A–F in Problems 3, 4 and 6. Ask for numbers 1–6 instead.

edits.quote: Two ruled lines under Problem 4 are the only recording space for a 4-flip round trip and the 5- and 7-flip answers.
edits.fix: Add four or five small copies of covering A, or the hexagon outline with its flippable spots marked, so children can record which hexagon they flip at each step.

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: The Problem 1 board is also a hexagon (with one top edge), so say 'On the board from Problem 3'.

grades-4-5.summary: A rich sequence on kernel 2. It covers the 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon and their flip graph (diameter 4), then pictured flip pairs whose distances check out at 3, 4 and 8. A 4-flip loop from A does exist, the ribbon example LRRLR is drawn correctly, the parity and lower-bound proofs are posed properly, and the two final counts are 20 and 20. Edits are small (a letter clash, an ambiguous 'the hexagon board', P4 recording space, the footer), and there is far more than forty minutes of work.

overall.strongest: The grades 2–3 part builds the up/down coloring obstruction through well-chosen contrasting boards (odd count, unbalanced even, balanced but disconnected, holes) up to fewest greens, chevrons, invention and a correct general rule.
overall.weakest: The weakest points are small: K–1 P3's ambiguous 'Make every shape a different way', a letter clash and too little P4 recording space in grades 4–5, and footers missing the required id on every page.
